items.title: Headlines for November 17, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: ## Trump Arrives in Philippines Ahead of ASEAN Summit and Meeting with Putin, Xi Nov 17, 2026 President Trump has arrived in the Philippines on the first leg of a 48-hour trip to Asia. Trump landed in Manila aboard the new Air Force One, a luxury 747 jet gifted to him by the government of Qatar. He’s scheduled to meet with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ahead of the ASEAN summit of Southeast Asian nations. Trump’s visit has drawn large protests in Manila, where police arrested hundreds of people over the weekend. Students, workers and progressive groups are demanding an end to the U.S. and Israeli war on Iran and are protesting against plans to build an artificial intelligence and manufacturing hub near Manila. On Thursday, Trump will hold an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump also said he might meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un while in China. ## Trump Says He “Would Not Mind” Seeing Jensen Huang Restored as CEO of Nvidia Nov 17, 2026 The Trump administration said Monday it would investigate Megaspeed, the Singapore-based cloud computing firm that’s accused of sending advanced Nvidia computer chips to China, in violation of U.S. export controls. The investigation follows Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO, after he admitted he’d had an extramarital affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. Megaspeed said on Sunday she had left the company more than a year ago. On Monday, President Trump responded to reports that Jensen Huang is in discussions with allies about a potential return to Nvidia. ... ## Trump Takes “No Responsibility” for Largest FAA Ground Stop Since 9/11 Nov 17, 2026 United Airlines canceled dozens of departing flights and delayed more than 800 others on Monday after a system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes. United blamed a “technical issue,” without elaborating, and said in a statement there was “no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.” This comes after the FAA ordered a nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop on Friday, causing over 18,000 flight cancellations and more than 28,000 delays. It was the largest disruption of its kind to U.S. air travel since the 9/11 attacks. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is due to brief senators about the incident today. On Monday, President Trump said Duffy had his full support, and blamed the Biden administration for the grounded flights. > President Donald Trump: “I don’t take any responsibility. They did a great job. Secretary Duffy, they acted incredibly. Everybody was safe. Nobody was hurt. No crashes, no nothing.” ... ## JPMorgan Chase Blames “Software Bug” After Customers Lose Access to Accounts and Services Nov 17, 2026 Customers at major U.S. banks lost access to their accounts for several hours on Monday, after JPMorgan Chase reported a “temporary issue related to a software bug.” The outage began around 10 a.m. Eastern time and continued until early evening. It left thousands of people unable to use the money transfer service Zelle and caused problems for customers at several other U.S. banks, including Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Bank of America. JPMorgan Chase said the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack. Meanwhile, Microsoft said Monday that last week’s global outage affecting services including Outlook, Teams and Copilot was due to a hidden defect in Microsoft’s cloud gateway, along with increased traffic demand and reduced server capacity. ## Israel Failed to Meet Commitments to Deliver Food and Supplies to Gaza Nov 17, 2026 In Gaza, Israeli forces killed a young Palestinian man and wounded others in an attack east of the city of Deir al-Balah in central Gaza. Elsewhere, Israeli forces killed one Palestinian and injured five in the north, while in southern Gaza, Israeli forces shot and wounded three Palestinians, including a child, inside a school. The latest killings come as Israel has failed to meet its aid commitments under the Gaza ceasefire deal. Data obtained by Haaretz showed decreasing food deliveries to Gaza, alongside severe shortages of medical supplies, tents and materials to repair damaged infrastructure. The U.N. is also urging the protection of aid workers and hospitals. This is U.N. spokesperson Farhan Haq. > Farhan Haq: “Yesterday, an Israeli airstrike hit very close to a U.N.-led fuel convoy in Rafah. We are concerned that strikes at targets near our staff and vehicles, especially vehicles carrying fuel, expose them to unacceptable risks. Civilians, including humanitarian workers, must always be protected.” ## Israeli Opposition Slams Netanyahu’s “Attempted Coup” over Framed Arab MKs ... ## Iran Attacks U.S. Radar Station in Bahrain, Says It Captured U.S. Drone Nov 17, 2026 Bahrain’s military says it intercepted an Iranian drone strike targeting a U.S. radar facility — the third attack of its kind in recent days. The assault came after U.S. Central Command announced a third carrier strike group, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, had arrived in the Middle East, adding about 10,000 sailors and Marines to U.S. forces in the region. Meanwhile, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it had hacked the flight guidance system of a U.S.-made MQM-170 drone and landed it remotely, intact. It’s the latest in a series of similar claims by Iran. Meanwhile, three more vessels caught fire while transiting the Strait of Hormuz today, including a ship carrying liquefied natural gas and a supertanker holding more than 2 million barrels of crude oil. ## Ukrainian Strike Damages Bridge Linking Crimea to Russia Russia reports that Ukraine has carried out its largest drone strike of the war so far. According to Moscow, the attack damaged the major bridge connecting Russia with occupied Crimea and struck several oil refineries. Russian officials say their forces shot down over 2,000 drones and four long-range Flamingo missiles in a 24-hour period. Moscow’s mayor said about 600 of those drones were aimed at the capital. Meanwhile, Kyiv had 17 air raid alerts in one day, the most on record. Russian strikes killed at least seven people in Ukraine, as attacks on energy infrastructure left 50,000 people without power.

items.title: Fed’s Musalem: US likely needs several rate hikes by spring to control inflation By Reuters
items.excerpt: Published Nov 17, 2026, 07:32 AM ... WASHINGTON, Nov 17 (Reuters) - The US Federal Reserve many need several rate hikes to bring high inflation under control and should act soon to ensure the problem doesn’t get worse, St. Louis Fed president Alberto Musalem said on Tuesday. "The economy will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027 to achieve price stability in a timely manner," Musalem said, arguing that the current policy rate, in the 3.75% to 4% range, is as much as a percentage point below where it needs to be to return inflation to the Fed’s 2% target. It is currently running above 3%, and Musalem said the most likely scenario is that it remains elevated unless the Fed acts. The Fed next meets on Dec. 8-9 and is expected to approve a quarter percentage point rate hike. Musalem is not a voter on interest rate policy this year. "Inflation is too high...Looking ahead, risks are skewed toward persistent above-target inflation," with current policy not acting as significant restraint on growth that continues above trend, Musalem said in remarks prepared for delivery to a Central Bank of Argentina conference in Buenos Aires. "Moving sooner, while inflation expectations are anchored, has a better chance of succeeding without adverse impact on the labor market or economic growth," he said.

items.title: US import prices rise more than expected in October By Reuters
items.excerpt: Published Nov 17, 2026, 09:10 AM Updated Nov 17, 2026, 09:12 AM ... WASHINGTON, Nov 17 (Reuters) - US import prices increased more than expected in October, the latest indication that inflation pressures were broadening beyond energy goods. Import prices advanced 1.1% last month after rising by the same margin in September, the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics said on Tuesday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast import prices, which exclude tariffs, climbing 0.7%. The BLS did not publish year-over-year import price readings because last year’s federal government shutdown prevented the collection of data in October 2025, leaving no comparison base. Imported inflation accelerated 8.1% in September, the largest gain in just more than four years. The government last week reported stronger-than-expected consumer prices in October as well as firmer producer inflation details, reinforcing economists’ views inflation was broadening beyond the energy sector as the US-Israeli war with Iran drags on. Economists expect the Federal Reserve to continue raising interest rates after next month’s widely expected hike. Financial markets have priced in a 25-basis-point rate hike in December and anticipated another increase in borrowing costs in January, CME’s FedWatch tool showed. The Fed left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range last month. Import prices were last month driven by a 3.6% rise in the cost of fuels. That followed a 6.3% jump in September. There were also increases in the prices of petroleum and natural gas. Imported food prices fell 0.2% after rising 0.4% in September. Excluding the fuels and food, import prices shot up 0.9% after increasing 0.5% in September. Prices of imported capital goods soared 1.5%, driven by a 1.7% jump in the cost of nonelectrical machinery. That is likely related to the AI infrastructure buildout. Imported capital goods prices advanced 1.0% in September. Imported automotive vehicles, parts and engines prices increased 0.4% after gaining 0.3% in September. Prices for consumer goods, excluding automotives, rose 0.5% after climbing 0.3% in September.

items.title: Is the Inflation Shock Starting to Lose Momentum? | Investing.com
items.excerpt: By James Picerno Published 11/17/2026, 07:37 AM There’s more to inflation than oil prices, but the recent pullback in crude suggests that the inflationary pressure tied to the Iran conflict may be starting to ease. Even if energy prices continue to move lower, it’s unclear how quickly that relief will filter through to broader inflation measures. Still, the growing possibility of such an outcome offers a measure of encouragement. Maybe, just maybe, a light at the end of the tunnel is beginning to come into view. Let’s start with the U.S. oil benchmark, West Texas Intermediate (WTI), which is trading near its lowest level since August at around $86 a barrel. A break lower from here would signal growing confidence that the market expects the Middle East supply shock to continue easing, at least relative to the worst days of the war. That confidence remains fragile, of course. In the blink of an eye, the U.S. or Iran could launch an attack that sends the optimists running for cover once again. It’s still premature to rule out that possibility, but the decline in oil prices suggests that optimism is gaining traction at the margin. The price of gasoline is also feeding expectations for eventual disinflation. The spot price recently fell to its lowest level since mid-March. More importantly, there are signs that diesel prices have peaked. As a key fuel for freight transportation and industrial activity, diesel exerts an outsized influence on costs across the economy. While the earlier surge in prices will continue to feed through to inflation in the near term, the recent downturn hints that the inflation shock is beginning to lose momentum. The pushback is that we’ve been here before, several times since the first attack on Feb. 28. It’s impossible to know whether we’re looking at another false dawn or a genuine inflection point in the inflation outlook. A key reason for caution is the unstable stalemate in the Middle East. ... Another reason for caution on the near-term disinflation outlook is the recent acceleration in U.S. economic growth, which appears set to continue in the fourth quarter. The Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow model estimates that output will rise at a 3.5% annualized pace in Q4. If correct, the pickup in growth that began in Q3 will continue, marking the strongest back-to-back quarters in more than a year. Stronger growth could keep inflation higher for longer by sustaining consumer demand and labor-market strength, limiting the economy’s ability to cool price pressures. That’s a meaningful concern with inflation still running well above the Fed’s 2% target, helping explain why markets expect another rate hike at next month’s FOMC meeting. Another round of policy tightening appears reasonable based on the Cleveland Fed’s nowcast for November consumer inflation, which projects the year-over-year CPI at the headline level will move close to 4% again. Higher inflation can help set the stage for its own decline. Rising prices squeeze household and business budgets, while higher interest rates increase borrowing costs. Together, those forces can cool demand, ease pressure on labor markets and supply chains, and ultimately slow the pace of price increases. For now, however, the odds of meaningful near-term relief on the inflation front appear low. Encouraging signs are beginning to emerge, particularly in energy markets, but it would be premature to declare victory. If oil and diesel prices resume their climb due to a new phase of conflict in the Middle East, the inflation outlook could deteriorate quickly.

items.title: Democrats’ Peltola ahead as counting nears end in Alaska Senate race – US politics live | US news | The Guardian
items.excerpt: ## Alaska midterm race could be called on Wednesday as Peltola remains ahead of Republican incumbent Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog. The final Senate race of this year’s midterm elections could be resolved tomorrow if Alaska election officials run the state’s ranked choice voting system to determine the result. With 98% of ballots counted, Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is out in front with 49.98% of the vote. By contrast, incumbent Republican senator Dan S Sullivan has a 45.93% share, according to the latest Associated Press figures. In terms of actual voting numbers, Peltola is ahead by just over 11,000, with 141,637 compared to Sullivan’s 130,162. All eyes will be on Peltola to see if she can keep the pace to achieve 50% of the ballot, two weeks on from the election. If not, then voters’ second choice votes will be counted. items.excerpt: 11/17/2026 4:45 AM EST In the days before the midterm election, Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) felt confident that a blue wave could open the door to immigration reform. Cuellar was so bullish that he reached out to acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement director David Venturella and the Customs and Border Protection commissioner Rodney Scott to feel out areas of “common ground,” he said in an interview. items.title: Morning News Brief - The Center Voter
items.excerpt: Federal Level Senate Confirms Domenico to Appeals Court in 51-46 Vote The Senate on Monday confirmed U.S. District Judge Daniel Domenico of Colorado to the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals by a vote of 51 to 46. Reuters reported that the vote leaves just three other appeals court nominees to confirm as Republicans work to fill judicial vacancies before Democrats take control of the chamber in January. Colorado’s Democratic senators, Michael Bennet and John Hickenlooper, voted against him. They had raised concerns about his broad view of the government’s immigration detention authority and his refusal to acknowledge President Trump’s loss in the 2020 election. Domenico will succeed Judge Timothy Tymkovich, for whom he once clerked. 1, 2 Senate Moves Permitting Bill Toward Final Passage Vote The Senate voted 70 to 27 on Monday to end debate on a substitute amendment to a bipartisan permitting reform bill, setting up a final Senate vote before the Thanksgiving recess. The amendment, sponsored by Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, strengthens provisions dealing with energy-hungry data centers and tribal sovereignty. The bill would speed the construction of energy, mining and infrastructure projects while limiting environmental challenges under several federal laws. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada has threatened to oppose a final vote unless a section affecting historic preservation is removed. The measure would still need to pass the House. 3 Trump Says He Takes No Responsibility for Ground Stop President Trump said Monday that he takes no responsibility for last week’s four-hour nationwide ground stop that disrupted thousands of flights. “I don’t take any responsibility,” Trump told reporters, adding that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and his team “acted incredibly.” The president said he worked from the Oval Office during the crisis and saw no reason to address the public himself. He again blamed prior administrations for outdated air traffic equipment and urged Congress to quickly approve more money for upgrades. Duffy has indicated he will ask for roughly $50 billion, and Democrats have questioned how existing funds are being spent. 4 ... Foxx Requests Recount in Close North Carolina House Race Rep. Virginia Foxx of North Carolina said Monday that she has requested a recount in her reelection race, where she trails Democrat Chuck Hubbard by 331 votes. Unofficial totals show Hubbard with 139,770 votes and Foxx with 139,439, a margin within the 1 percent that state law allows for a recount. Foxx, an 11-term Republican, is the only Republican congressional candidate in the state to seek one. She said in a statement that she expects a smooth process that respects state law. The state elections board plans to finish a machine recount by Nov. 23 and to consider certification on Nov. 24. 6, 7 Van Hollen Says Bid to Replace Schumer Is Gaining Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Monday that his challenge to Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer is gaining momentum. “Well, I’m the underdog, but we are really moving in the right direction here,” Van Hollen told NPR’s Morning Edition. He argued that Democratic leaders should stay out of contested primaries, pointing to incoming Sens. Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota. He also called for an end to further funding for the war in Iran. Schumer says he has enough votes to remain leader, and the winner will need close to 30 votes in a secret ballot. 8 Khanna Urges Democrats to Pass Iran War Refund Checks Rep. Ro Khanna of California called on Monday for Democrats to pass $1,700 refund checks for Americans during their first week in control of Congress in January. “The first week in January, the House and Senate must pass a $1,700 refund check to Americans,” Khanna said in a statement. He introduced the Illegal War Refund Act in September to offset higher fuel prices, food prices and other costs he links to the Iran war. The bill drew four co-sponsors and was referred to House committees without further action. Democrats will hold at least 256 House seats and 55 Senate seats in the new Congress. 9

Harry Styles did not receive a nomination and Noah Kahan only received one. Beyoncé makes history with her 100th career nomination. Dolly Parton and Tim Curry receive posthumous nominations.
